title: The Unfinished Building on Ngong Road Where Lancet Kenya Began
dek: In 2009 the pathologist Ahmed Kalebi opened a private laboratory in Nairobi on a contractor's generator, after his plan to build one with the government stalled.

story.company: Pathologists Lancet Kenya (later Cerba Lancet Kenya)
story.event: Opening Lancet Kenya's first laboratory in Nairobi with a South African partner
story.summary: In 2009 the Kenyan pathologist Ahmed Kalebi opened Pathologists Lancet Kenya in the unfinished Fifth Avenue building on Ngong Road, Nairobi, with funding from the South African group Lancet Laboratories, whose chairman made him partner and chief executive after Kalebi's hope of building a referral laboratory with the government stalled. He did nearly every job himself at first; by his account the main laboratory was accredited by SANAS within its first year, and by 2017 Lancet had about 40 branches in four East African countries.
paragraphs: In 2009 a new laboratory moved into Fifth Avenue, an unfinished building on Ngong Road in Nairobi, near Kenyatta National Hospital. It ran on the building contractor's generator. Its founder, the pathologist Ahmed Kalebi, who grew up in Kibra, later described his job there: "When we started this place I was the pathologist, project manager, lab manager, finance guy, you know everything." By day he dealt with the tax office, Kenya Power and the bank. Nights, he said, were for his microscope slides.

The idea had started in Garissa. After a master's in pathology at the University of Nairobi, he was posted there by the government, became the first pathologist at its provincial hospital and helped set up the district's first proper laboratory. He later said it troubled him that people there waited weeks for routine tests, and that "one case of leukaemia particularly broke my heart": a patient lost a few weeks after he arrived. He went on to a pathology fellowship at the University of the Witwatersrand in Johannesburg.

His first plan was public. He wanted to build a modern referral laboratory with the government and approached the Ministry of Health, but, he said, "resources were constrained" and the paperwork dragged. Near the end of his studies, in 2008 by his account, Dr Gangaram Hariparsad, chairman of the South African pathology group Lancet Laboratories, called him. Hariparsad offered the money and made Kalebi a partner and chief executive, with a minority stake. Kalebi took it. When they started, he said later, Kenya had no clear regulations for that kind of laboratory work.

Lancet Kenya started with 25 staff. By Kalebi's account, its main laboratory was accredited by South Africa's national accreditation body within its first year. By 2014 it employed 312 people across East Africa, and by mid-2017 it had about 40 branches in Kenya, Uganda, Rwanda and Tanzania, six facilities holding international accreditation. He said he sometimes worked 23 hours a day, and sometimes stayed two days without going home, his wife bringing him a change of clothes. His turning point, he said, came when "the home front was suffering". In 2019 the French group Cerba HealthCare took majority control of Lancet's business outside South Africa. Kalebi retired as chief executive in April 2021.

quote.text: If, sometimes, I have been put upon the management of other men's affairs, I have promised to take them in hand, but not into my lungs and liver; to take them upon me, not to incorporate them; to take pains, yes: to be impassioned about it, by no means
quote.locator: Book III, Chapter X, "Of Managing the Will"
quote.translator: Charles Cotton (1685), ed. W. C. Hazlitt
quote.source_title: Essays of Michel de Montaigne — Complete, tr. Charles Cotton, Project Gutenberg eBook #3600
quote.connection: Montaigne, given charge of other people's affairs, promised them his effort but not his whole self. Kalebi, running a laboratory mostly owned by others, gave it 23-hour days, and the patient in Garissa is part of the reason. Montaigne's rule and Kalebi's cause pull in different directions, and both have weight.

reflection: Kalebi's reasons were concrete. He had seen a patient lost to a late diagnosis, and he built a laboratory that, by his account, was accredited before its first birthday. It is hard to read that and then say he should have cared less.

Montaigne does not ask for less care, only for a line between taking pains and taking the work into your body. You know that pull: talQen exists because you have seen what a slow or careless result costs someone. The work deserves your pains. It does not need your sleep, and Kalebi's own turning point came when he noticed who else was paying for it.
invitation: This morning, choose the time you will stop work tonight, and tell one person at home what it is.

cross_checks.claim: Kalebi founded Lancet Kenya in 2009 as an offshoot of the South African Lancet Laboratories
The first laboratory was in the Fifth Avenue building on Ngong Road, Nairobi
Before Lancet he was a government pathologist in Garissa and trained further in South Africa
The decision: his attempt to work with the government stalled, and Lancet's South African chairman offered funding and a partnership

research_notes: The slate dated the founding to 2007; every source gives 2009 (Business Daily 2014 and 2017, Nation 2019, Business Daily 2021, which dates his contract from May 2009), so the story uses 2009 and Kalebi's 2008 for the first call from Lancet's chairman. Funding: the slate said bootstrapped, but Kalebi's own account (Business Daily 2014, The Star) is that Lancet Laboratories of South Africa funded the venture and made him partner and CEO; Business Daily 2024 calls him founder and minority shareholder, and Business Daily 2021 gives his stake as 7.67% of PLK and 10% of Lancet Services Company. The Standard's joint-venture interview says his unchanged holding made him the largest single shareholder in Lancet Kenya; the story says only that his stake was a minority one. Business Daily (16 March 2021) says he founded PLK 'before it was acquired by French and South African partners', which conflicts with his own account of South African funding from the start; the story follows his account. Outcome numbers: Business Daily 2021 credits him with growing 'the group' to more than 100 laboratories in 11 African countries, but the Standard's joint-venture report gives 100-plus laboratories in 11 countries as the whole of Cerba-Lancet Africa outside South Africa, while Kalebi's own East African group covered four countries (The Star). The story uses the narrower July 2017 figure of about 40 branches in four countries, reported by both Business Daily and the Standard. Jackson Biko's May 2017 profile instead says Lancet had opened 16 more laboratories across 17 counties; it is not used. Staff figures (25 in 2009, 312 in 2014) come from Business Daily 2014 only; Nation 2019 gives more than 600 employees. Accreditation: the claim that the main laboratory was accredited by SANAS within its first year is Kalebi's own (The Star) and is attributed to him; a Cerba Lancet job advert says 'since 2010' but is not cited. Departure: contemporary reports (Business Daily, 11 and 16 March 2021; the Standard, 23 March 2021) have him retiring as group MD and CEO on 30 April 2021 after announcing it in March; Business Daily (2024) says he stayed until 2018 and then took a three-year sabbatical, during which he fell out with the new majority shareholders. The story follows the 2021 reports. The Star interview's URL is dated 7 March 2016 but the page shows 20 January 2019. Kalebi's 23-hour days and his wife bringing clothes come from his 2017 interview with Biko. The Montaigne passage comes from the essay in which he goes on to describe his time as mayor of Bordeaux; it is applied here by analogy.
